Issued at 1220 PM CST Mon Nov 16 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: A gusty southwesterly wind continues through the 
region this afternoon.  Lingering stratus through the CWA remains a 
good hint that sufficient low-lvl moisture has advected northward 
into the region, now trapped by increasing WAA above it. Morning 
soundings from LBF/OAX both showed an increase in the depth of 
moisture around the 900:850 mb layer, with satellite showing 
expanding and advecting stratus northward. 

TONIGHT: The surface pressure gradient remains strong overnight, 
however the natural decoupling of the lower levels should limit the 
sustained strong gusts to just the higher elevations of the Buffalo 
Ridge. Some guidance is split on the the prevalence of stratus 
tonight, but given satellite trends and continued advection of the 
moisture in the cloud bearing  layer, would expect more stratus 
develop into Tuesday morning. Additionally, increasing mid-lvl 
moisture and the upper jet positioning should increase mid-upr 
cloud layers. 

TUESDAY: With deepening upper troughing moving into the Rockies, the 
SPG will not relax at all on Tuesday, in fact, sustained winds 
and gusts may actually increase through the day. With some CAMs 
hinting at 40-45 mph gusts at times, some caution will be needed
as stratus has the potential to hang around and could limit the
overall depth of mixing. The other concern for Tuesday will be 
with temperatures should stratus develop and hang around through
the day like what's happening in central and southern Nebraska.
The spread in the NBM remains between 52-57 degrees, but the 
NBM also has minimal cloud cover. While the HRRR/RAP may be too 
cool generally, they are short term models that suggest 
widespread stratus Tuesday. The result in this scenario would be
for high temperatures in the middle to upper 40s. 

WEDNESDAY: The aforementioned upper trough ejects out of the Rockies 
late Tuesday night, heading into the Northern Plains on 
Wednesday. Low-lvl winds increase further on Wednesday with >60%
probabilities of 40+ mph winds along the higher elevation areas
through the middle of the day. A localized wind advisory may be
needed for the Buffalo Ridge area Tuesday night and early 
Wednesday. 

As surface cyclogenesis takes place over the western Dakotas early 
WEdnesday, this surface low is anticipated to track through North 
Dakota in the afternoon. A quasi-dryline will surge east through 
the CWA in the afternoon, with a true cold front catching up to 
the boundary by the evening hours east of I-29. For those 
looking for precipitation, this system will be rather moisture 
starved as the Texas Panhandle, not the Gulf, will serve as the 
moisture source region. Thus, PoPs into Wednesday night are 
likely to stay very low. 

THURSDAY-FRIDAY: The passage of the upper trough along the Canada 
border will not bring substancial chances to the Tri-State area for 
the end of the week. Temperatures will cool slightly behind the
boundary but are expected to remain in the 50s. Another upper 
trough dropping into the Western CONUS will induce stronger 
return flow and potentially open up the Gulf for deeper moisture
advection by Friday. The northward advection of low-lvl 
moisture behind a passing warm front Friday should bring a 
return of stratus and perhaps even drizzle to light rain by 
Friday afternoon/night. 

SATURDAY-SUNDAY: This second trough will pose some monitoring for 
the potential for precipitation into the upcoming weekend, however 
considerable model spread remains at this time period. The 
greatest uncertainty will be focused on the overall storm track 
through the Plains. Given the open nature of the wave at this 
point in the forecast, this would favor the greatest potential 
for precipitation along most of North Dakota into northern 
Minnesota, with a secondary increased area for precipitation 
(perhaps even convection) along an elongated frontal boundary 
through the Tri- State area. Higher forecast confidence exists 
in the expected drop in temperatures by the end of the weekend 
and early next week. Both ECMWF/GEFS show nearly 50% 
probabilities of high temperatures near or below 40 degrees 
Sunday and Monday.
